title: Study Design I — Observational Designs — Test

mcqs.q: A research study design is best described as:
opts: A framework and blueprint for how the researcher collects, measures and analyzes data
The statistical test chosen after data collection
The ethical approval document
The list of variables measured in a study
mcqs.explain: It is the method or process by which researchers organize their projects so the research answers the question at hand.

mcqs.q: An exposure variable is:
opts: A risk factor participants already have, which the researcher only observes
A treatment deliberately assigned by the researchers
The clinical event that develops as a consequence
A characteristic describing only the demographic profile
mcqs.explain: It is the independent or predictor variable, and the researcher does not assign it.

mcqs.q: In a study of stroke prevention in adults with hypertension, smoking and pre-existing beta-blocker use are:
opts: Exposure variables
Intervention variables
Outcome variables
Confounding variables by definition
mcqs.explain: They are characteristics participants already have, which the researcher observes rather than assigns.

mcqs.q: An intervention variable is:
opts: A treatment, procedure or action deliberately assigned to participants by the researchers
A risk factor participants already have
The outcome that develops as a consequence
A background demographic characteristic
mcqs.explain: It is part of an experimental study such as a randomized controlled trial.

mcqs.q: The key difference between an exposure and an intervention is that:
opts: With exposure the researcher observes what happened; with intervention, assigns it
An exposure is always harmful and an intervention always beneficial
Exposures are measured whereas interventions are only estimated
An exposure is a dependent and an intervention an independent variable
mcqs.explain: Both are independent or predictor variables; only the researcher's role differs.

mcqs.q: The outcome variable is:
opts: The clinical event or measurement developing as a consequence of the exposure
The risk factor whose effect is being studied in the research
The treatment assigned by the research team to participants
The inclusion criterion used in selecting the sample
mcqs.explain: It is what researchers measure to see if the predictor variable made a difference.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a stated consideration when choosing a study design?
opts: The likely impact factor of the publishing journal
The aim of the study
The resources available — time, personnel and finance
Ethical considerations — participant safety and regulatory approval
mcqs.explain: The advantages and disadvantages of each design are the fourth consideration.

mcqs.q: Which design belongs to the DESCRIPTIVE observational group?
opts: Case series
Case-control
Cohort
Randomized controlled trial
mcqs.explain: The descriptive group is case report, case series, correlation (ecological) and survey (cross-sectional).

mcqs.q: Which study design appears in BOTH the descriptive and the analytic observational columns?
opts: Cross-sectional
Case report
Cohort
Case-control
mcqs.explain: A cross-sectional study can either describe a population or test associations.

mcqs.q: Both diagnostic and therapeutic interventional designs may be called:
opts: A clinical trial
A cohort study
An ecological study
A case series
mcqs.explain: The interventional group listed is preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic.

mcqs.q: In an observational study:
opts: The researcher documents a naturally occurring relationship and does not intervene
The researcher assigns participants to treatment groups
Randomization is always used
A placebo is always required
mcqs.explain: The exposure has already been decided naturally or by some other factor.

mcqs.q: Comparing the incidence of lung cancer in smokers versus non-smokers is an example of:
opts: An observational study
An interventional study
A randomized controlled trial
A quasi-experimental study
mcqs.explain: The researcher does not assign smoking; it is observed.

mcqs.q: A descriptive study is designed to:
opts: Describe the distribution of one or more variables, without regard to any causal or other hypothesis
Test whether an exposure causes an outcome
Compare a treatment with a placebo
Calculate relative risk
mcqs.explain: Its types are case report, case series, cross-sectional and ecological.

mcqs.q: Which descriptive design uses AGGREGATED data for groups rather than data on individuals?
opts: The ecological study
The case report
The case series
The cross-sectional study
mcqs.explain: The first three collect data on individuals; the ecological study uses group averages.

mcqs.q: A case report is:
opts: A patient with an unusual disease, or more than one condition at once
An aggregation of multiple similar cases over time
A comparison of cases with matched controls
A follow-up of an exposed and a non-exposed group
mcqs.explain: A case series is the aggregation of multiple, often only a few, similar cases.

mcqs.q: HIV/AIDS was first recognized through:
opts: A case report of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma and a case series of young men with pneumonia
A large prospective cohort study
An ecological correlation across countries
A randomized controlled trial
mcqs.explain: It is the classic illustration of case reports and series generating a hypothesis.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of case reports and case series?
opts: They act as triggers, stimulating analytic studies to identify risk factors
They can test the presence or absence of an association
They control for confounding factors
They provide a direct estimate of relative risk
mcqs.explain: They also identify new cases, formulate hypotheses, and can supply cases for a case-control study.

mcqs.q: The fundamental limitation shared by the case report and the case series is:
opts: The lack of a comparison group, so they cannot test the presence or absence of an association
That they take too long to conduct
That they require a very large sample
That they cannot be published
mcqs.explain: The case report also rests on one person's experience, and the exposure may be coincidental.

mcqs.q: An ecological (correlational) study looks for an association between exposure and outcome:
opts: Across populations rather than in individuals
Within matched pairs of individuals
Between treated and untreated patients
Before and after an intervention in the same person
mcqs.explain: It uses averages for both exposure and disease.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the ecological study?
opts: It is quick and inexpensive because it uses already available data
It proves causation
It controls for confounding
It links exposure to disease in a particular individual
mcqs.explain: Its second advantage is that it generates hypotheses.

mcqs.q: Why can an ecological study never link exposure and disease in a particular individual?
opts: Because averages are used for both exposure and disease
Because participants are anonymous
Because it uses only questionnaires
Because the data are collected prospectively
mcqs.explain: This is the core limitation of using aggregated group data.

mcqs.q: A confounding factor is defined as:
opts: A factor other than the exposure that disturbs its relation with the disease
The outcome variable being measured in the study
Any variable that is measured at baseline
The treatment assigned by the researcher
mcqs.explain: Ecological studies lack the ability to control for confounders.

mcqs.q: In a cross-sectional study, exposure and outcome are:
opts: Measured at the same time in the study participants
Measured before and after an intervention
Assessed backward from the outcome
Followed forward from the exposure
mcqs.explain: This single feature explains both the advantages and disadvantages of the design.

mcqs.q: Cross-sectional designs are commonly used for:
opts: Population-based surveys and assessing prevalence of diseases in clinic-based samples
Establishing causation between exposure and outcome
Calculating incidence rates
Evaluating rare diseases
mcqs.explain: Prevalence, not incidence, is what a cross-sectional study estimates.

mcqs.q: A descriptive cross-sectional design mainly aims to:
opts: Give a clear picture of the situation — percentages, averages, distributions, profiles
Test a complex explanation using regression models
Track how the very same individuals change over time
Compare a treated group with an untreated group
mcqs.explain: Its results should be read as descriptions of the measured period and sample.

mcqs.q: An analytical cross-sectional design:
opts: Examines relationships between variables and may use regression to adjust for background variables
Only reports percentages and averages
Follows the same people over several years
Requires randomization of participants
mcqs.explain: For example, examining whether study environment, sleep duration and attendance are associated with exam performance.

mcqs.q: A repeated cross-sectional design:
opts: Collects data at more than one time point, but not necessarily from the same people
Follows exactly the same individuals over time
Measures exposure only once and outcome twice
Requires a control group
mcqs.explain: Each wave is a new snapshot, so it shows population trends but not individual change.

mcqs.q: A national survey asks a new sample of students every two years about reading habits. This design:
opts: Can show whether the population percentage changed, not how individuals changed
Can show how each individual student's habits changed over time
Is in fact a form of prospective cohort study
Establishes that reading causes better academic performance
mcqs.explain: Individual change requires following the same students.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the cross-sectional study?
opts: We can estimate the prevalence of disease
We can calculate incidence rates
We can establish causation
It is suitable for rare diseases
mcqs.explain: It may also be conducted before planning a cohort study or as a baseline within one.

mcqs.q: The “chicken-and-egg dilemma” of the cross-sectional study means:
opts: Exposure and outcome are measured at one time, so causality is hard to derive
The sample size in such studies is always too small
Cases and controls are typically poorly matched
The period of follow-up is invariably too short
mcqs.explain: There is no way to tell which came first.

mcqs.q: The statement that cross-sectional data “deal with survivors” means:
opts: Those who died or were cured are not included
Only elderly participants are enrolled
Only treated patients are studied
Only incident cases are captured
mcqs.explain: This is one of the four listed disadvantages, along with unsuitability for acute short-duration and rare diseases.

mcqs.q: A case-control study:
opts: Compares those with an outcome against those without, looking back at exposures
Follows exposed and non-exposed groups forward in time
Assigns participants to either treatment or placebo
Measures exposure and outcome at the same moment
mcqs.explain: Researchers start with the outcome and look backward in time.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the case-control study?
opts: It is suitable for rare diseases and requires few subjects
It is suitable for rare exposures
It provides a direct estimate of incidence
It is free from recall bias
mcqs.explain: It is also easy, rapid and cheap, can examine multiple etiologic factors for one disease, allows estimation of risk, has no attrition problem and faces minimal ethical problems.

mcqs.q: The case-control design is characteristically able to examine:
opts: Multiple etiologic factors for a single disease
Multiple diseases arising from a single exposure
Incidence in exposed and non-exposed groups
The effect of a newly assigned treatment
mcqs.explain: Examining multiple effects of one exposure is the strength of the cohort design instead.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the case-control study?
opts: Unsuitable for rare exposures, and bias is commoner than in other analytic designs
It suffers from a serious problem of attrition
It is extremely expensive and time consuming
It cannot estimate risk under any circumstances
mcqs.explain: No attrition problem and low cost are among its advantages.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four listed types of bias in case-control studies?
opts: Attrition bias
Recall bias
Interviewer bias
Selection bias
mcqs.explain: The fourth listed is bias due to confounding factors, which should be controlled by the control group.

mcqs.q: Recall bias arises in a case-control study because:
opts: Cases, knowing they are ill, remember past exposures differently from controls
Interviewers question cases more thoroughly
Controls are chosen from a different population
Participants drop out during follow-up
mcqs.explain: The design starts from the outcome and looks backward, which builds this bias in.

mcqs.q: A cohort study selects individuals on the basis of:
opts: Being exposed or non-exposed, then follows them to see whether the disease develops
Having or not having the disease, then looks backward at exposure
A single measurement of exposure and outcome together
Random assignment to treatment or placebo
mcqs.explain: Groups are identified at the beginning, followed over time, and their outcomes compared.

mcqs.q: The difference between a prospective and a retrospective cohort is that:
opts: In the retrospective cohort both the starting exposure and the follow-up are past
The retrospective cohort starts from the outcome and looks backward
The prospective cohort uses only pre-existing records
The retrospective cohort design requires randomization
mcqs.explain: Both move forward from exposure to outcome; only where the researcher stands on the timeline differs.

mcqs.q: Which measure can be calculated from a cohort study but NOT from a case-control study?
opts: Incidence rate and hence a direct estimate of relative and attributable risk
Odds ratio
Prevalence at one time point
Frequency of exposure in cases
mcqs.explain: Only a cohort starts from exposure and watches the disease appear.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the cohort study?
opts: No selection bias, because exposure is assessed before the disease occurs
It is cheap and rapid
It is ideal for rare diseases
It has no attrition problem
mcqs.explain: Because exposure is assessed first, the outcomes cannot influence the selection of the exposure.

mcqs.q: The cohort design is characteristically able to examine:
opts: Multiple effects of one exposure — smoking causing CHD, cancers, ulcer, hypertension
Multiple causes of one single rare disease
Exposure and outcome at a single point in time
Group-level averages compared across populations
mcqs.explain: Multiple causes of one disease is the strength of the case-control design.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the retrospective cohort specifically?
opts: The records are unavailable and incomplete, and it is not accurate
Participants may migrate or die during follow-up
It is the most expensive design
It cannot estimate relative risk
mcqs.explain: Loss of participants during follow-up is a limitation of the prospective cohort.

mcqs.q: The attrition problem in a prospective cohort refers to:
opts: Loss of participants by migration, death or lost interest, affecting validity
Loss of experienced staff over the study period
Loss of the funding supporting the study
Change in the standard diagnostic criteria
mcqs.explain: Loss of staff, funds, changing environmental factors and changing diagnostic criteria are the other prospective-cohort limitations.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is CORRECT?
opts: Case-control suits rare diseases; cohort suits rare exposures
Case-control suits rare exposures; cohort suits rare diseases
Both suit rare diseases equally
Neither is suitable for rare conditions
mcqs.explain: This mirror-image relationship is the fastest way to choose between the two analytic designs.

saqs.q: Define a research study design and distinguish between exposure, intervention and outcome variables.
saqs.a: A STUDY DESIGN is the framework by which researchers organize a project — a blueprint for collecting, measuring and analyzing data so the research answers the question. EXPOSURE (independent/predictor) — a risk factor participants already have; the researcher observes, does not assign (smoking, pre-existing beta-blocker use). INTERVENTION (also independent) — a treatment deliberately assigned by the researchers (a new antihypertensive randomly assigned). OUTCOME (dependent) — the clinical event or measurement that develops as a consequence (incidence of stroke within five years).

ans.text: A research study design is the framework by which researchers organize a project — a blueprint for how data are collected, measured and analyzed, ensuring the research answers the question at hand.

head: Variable
What it is
Example
rows:
EXPOSURE
independent / predictor
a risk factor or characteristic participants already have — the researcher observes and measures, does not assign
smoking · pre-existing beta-blocker use

INTERVENTION

a treatment, procedure or action deliberately assigned by the researchers, as in an RCT — actively controlled to test its effect
a new antihypertensive randomly assigned to 300, with 300 on placebo

OUTCOME
dependent
the clinical event, health state or measurement that develops as a consequence — what is measured to see if the predictor made a difference
incidence of acute ischemic stroke within five years (yes/no, or time to event)

saqs.q: Give the classification of research study designs and explain the difference between observational and interventional designs.
saqs.a: OBSERVATIONAL — descriptive (case report, case series, correlation/ecological, survey/cross-sectional) and analytic (cross-sectional, case-control, cohort). INTERVENTIONAL — preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic; diagnostic and therapeutic may be called a clinical trial. In OBSERVATIONAL studies the researcher documents a naturally occurring relationship with NO active intervention — exposure was decided naturally. In INTERVENTIONAL studies the researcher actively performs an intervention — a drug, vaccine, procedure or educational tool.

Designs

OBSERVATIONAL — analytic
cross-sectional · case-control · cohort
INTERVENTIONAL
preventive · diagnostic · therapeutic (intervention) — diagnostic and therapeutic may both be called a clinical trial

INTERVENTIONAL

the researcher actively performs an intervention in some or all participants — a drug or vaccine, a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure, or an educational tool

saqs.q: Describe case reports and case series, with their advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: CASE REPORT — the description of a patient with an unusual disease, or more than one condition at once. CASE SERIES — an aggregation of multiple, often few, similar cases. HIV/AIDS was first recognized through a case report of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma and a case series of men with pneumonia. ADVANTAGES — identify a new case or unusual variation; formulate a new hypothesis; trigger analytic studies; cases may be reused in a case-control study. DISADVANTAGES — based on one person's experience; exposure may be coincidental; no comparison group, so an association may be wrongly suggested or excluded; neither can test for an association.

head: CASE REPORT
CASE SERIES
rows: the description of a patient with an unusual disease, or the simultaneous occurrence of more than one condition
the same, but an aggregation of multiple — often only a few — similar cases

ans.text: Example — HIV/AIDS was first recognized through a case report of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma in a young homosexual man, and a case series of such men with pneumonia.

Disadvantages

saqs.q: Describe the ecological (correlational) study design with its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: The ECOLOGICAL (correlational) design looks for an association between exposure and outcome ACROSS POPULATIONS rather than in individuals. ADVANTAGES — quick and inexpensive, using already available data; generates hypotheses. DISADVANTAGES — cannot test the hypothesis, never proves causation; impossible to link exposure and disease in a particular individual, since averages are used; lacks the ability to control confounding factors.

ans.text: Looks for an association between an exposure and an outcome across populations rather than in individuals.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: quick and inexpensive — uses already available data
cannot test the hypothesis — it never proves causation
generates hypotheses
impossible to link exposure and disease in a particular individual, because averages are used
lacks the ability to control confounding factors — factors other than the studied exposure that disturb its relation with disease

saqs.q: Describe the cross-sectional study, its three forms, and its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: CROSS-SECTIONAL research studies a population at ONE POINT IN TIME, measuring outcome and exposures simultaneously, to describe features, estimate prevalence, compare groups or examine associations. FORMS — descriptive (a clear picture, percentages and profiles), analytical (relationships, comparisons, adjusted models, regression), repeated (several time points, not the same people, so each wave is a new snapshot). ADVANTAGES — relatively fast and inexpensive; usable before or as a baseline for a cohort; gives prevalence of outcomes or exposures. DISADVANTAGES — the chicken-and-egg dilemma, so causality is hard; deals with survivors; unusable in acute short diseases; unsuitable for rare diseases.

ans.text: Studying a defined population or sample at one point in time to describe features, estimate prevalence, compare groups or examine associations — the investigator measures the outcome and the exposures at the same time. Used for population-based surveys and prevalence in clinic-based samples.

head: Form
What it does
rows: DESCRIPTIVE
describes a population at one time — percentages, averages, distributions, categories or profiles. Aim is not to test a complex explanation but to give a clear picture
ANALYTICAL
examines relationships between variables — compares groups, tests associations, estimates adjusted relationships, builds models, possibly with regression
REPEATED
data at more than one time point but not necessarily from the same people — each wave is a new snapshot. Shows whether a population percentage has changed, not how the same individuals changed

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: relatively fast and inexpensive
the chicken-and-egg dilemma — one-time measurement makes causal relationships hard to derive
can precede, or form the baseline of, a cohort study
the data deal with survivors — those who died or were cured are not included
gives the prevalence of outcomes or exposures, useful for designing the cohort
cannot be used in acute diseases of short duration; unsuitable for rare diseases

saqs.q: Describe the case-control study, with its advantages, disadvantages and types of bias.
saqs.a: A CASE-CONTROL study compares people WITH the outcome (cases) against people WITHOUT it (controls), starting from the outcome and looking BACKWARD at past exposures. ADVANTAGES — easy, rapid and cheap; suitable for rare diseases; few subjects; examines multiple etiologic factors for one disease; allows estimation of risk; no attrition; minimal ethical problems. DISADVANTAGES — not suitable for rare EXPOSURES; bias is more common than in other analytic designs. BIASES — recall, interviewer, selection, and confounding (controlled by the control group).

ans.text: An observational design comparing people who have a particular outcome (cases) with people who do not (controls), to identify associated factors. Researchers start with the outcome and look backward in time at past exposures.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: easy, rapid and cheap compared with a prospective cohort
not suitable for rare exposures
suitable for rare diseases; requires few subjects
the problem of bias is more common than in other analytic designs
examines multiple etiologic factors for a single disease — smoking, exercise, stress and blood lipids in CHD
allows estimation of risk; no attrition problem; minimal ethical problems

list: Bias due to confounding factors — controlled by the control group

saqs.q: Describe the cohort study, its two types, the rates it yields, and its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: A COHORT study selects individuals by EXPOSED or NON-EXPOSED status and follows them to see whether disease develops. TYPES — prospective (starts with normal people, follow-up in the future) and retrospective (starts with normal people, but the exposure is in the past and the follow-up is also in the past). RATES — incidence rate (absolute risk), relative risk, attributable risk (risk difference). ADVANTAGES — valuable when the exposure is rare; examines multiple effects of one exposure; gives incidence in exposed and non-exposed; direct estimate of relative and attributable risk; no selection bias; allows hypothesis testing. DISADVANTAGES — unsuitable for rare diseases; retrospective limited by incomplete records; prospective limited by loss of staff and funds, changing environment and diagnostic criteria, attrition and ethical problems, and is expensive and time consuming.

ans.text: Individuals are selected on the basis of being exposed or non-exposed and followed for a period to determine whether the disease develops — groups identified at the start, followed over years or decades, and their outcomes compared.

head: Type
Starting point and follow-up
rows: PROSPECTIVE
starts with normal people (exposed or control) and follows up in the future
RETROSPECTIVE
also starts with normal people, exposed or not — but the starting exposure is in the past and the follow-up is also in the past

Disadvantages

not suitable for rare diseases

the retrospective cohort is limited by records that are unavailable, incomplete or inaccurate
gives incidence in exposed and non-exposed; direct estimate of relative and attributable risk
the prospective cohort is limited by loss of experienced staff and funds, changing environmental factors and diagnostic criteria
no selection bias — exposure is assessed before the disease occurs; allows hypothesis testing
